<translation>
<pb n="39"/>In the language of India: <term>Yuktiṣaṣṭikākārikā-nāma</term> <gloss>The Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning</gloss>.
In the language of Tibet: <term>Rigs pa drug cu pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa zhes bya ba</term>.
Homage to Manjushri, the Youthful.

I prostrate to the King of Sages <note>the Buddha</note>,
Who taught dependent origination,
The method by which
Birth and destruction are abandoned.

Those whose minds have transcended
Existence and non-existence, and who do not remain in them,
Realize the profound meaning of conditionality,
Which is free from any focal point.

Since the state of non-existence, the source of all faults,
Has already been turned away,
Listen now to how the state of existence
Is turned away through reasoning.

If things were true
In the way that children imagine them,
Why would one not desire liberation
Since those things would then be non-existent? <note>Implying that if things had inherent existence, their cessation would be total annihilation, which is not what liberation means.</note>

One is not liberated through existence,
Nor from this cyclic existence through non-existence.
By thoroughly knowing existence and non-existence,
The Great Beings are liberated.

Those who do not see suchness
Conceive of the world and <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>liberation from suffering</gloss>;
Those who see suchness
Do not conceive of the world and nirvana.

Existence and nirvana
Neither of these two exists.
The thorough knowledge of existence itself
Is what is called nirvana.

Just as the cessation of a thing
Is imagined when it has arisen and then perished,
So too do the Sublime Ones
Accept cessation like a magical illusion.

Cessation occurs through thorough knowledge of the conditioned,
Not through a process of destruction.
To whom would that be manifest?
How could there be knowledge of what has perished?

If the <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of body and mind</gloss> did not cease,
One would not transcend even if afflictions were exhausted.
When they have ceased here in this very life,
At that time one becomes liberated.

When one sees with perfect wisdom
What arises through the condition of ignorance,
Neither arising
Nor even cessation can be perceived.

That is nirvana seen in this very life,
The task is accomplished and done.
If there were any distinction in this
Following the knowledge of phenomena,

One who imagines birth
Even in the most subtle of things,
Is unwise and
Has not seen the meaning of what arises from conditions.

<pb n="40"/>If cyclic existence turned away
For a monk whose afflictions were exhausted,
Why would the Perfect Buddhas
Not describe its beginning?

If there were a beginning,
Then certainly views would be grasped.
How could there be a first or a last
In that which is dependently originated?

How could what has previously arisen
Be turned away again later?
The world, free from the extremes of beginning and end,
Appears like a magical illusion.

When one knows the illusion, one is not confused
By thinking, "When does the illusion arise?"
Or, "When does it perish?"
Those who do not know the illusion are completely attached to it.

When the mind sees existence
As being like a mirage or an illusion,
One is not corrupted by views
Of a beginning or an end.

Those who imagine birth and destruction
Regarding conditioned things,
Do not understand the movement of the world
According to the wheel of dependent origination.

That which arises in dependence on this or that
Has not arisen as its own inherent nature.
How can that which has not arisen
As its own inherent nature be said to "arise"?

The peace resulting from the exhaustion of causes
Is conceptualized as "exhaustion,"
But how can that which is not exhausted by nature
Be called "exhausted"?

Thus, nothing at all arises,
And nothing at all will cease.
The acts of arising and destruction
Were taught for a purposeful meaning. <note>taught as conventional truths for the sake of guiding students</note>

By knowing arising, one knows destruction;
By knowing destruction, one knows impermanence.
By knowing how to enter into impermanence itself,
One will also realize the Sublime Dharma.

Those who have come to know
Dependent origination as being
Free from arising and destruction,
Have crossed the ocean of existence.

Ordinary beings, identifying with things,
Are inverted regarding existence and non-existence.
Under the power of afflictions and faults,
They are deceived by their own minds.

Those who are skilled in the nature of things
See that things are impermanent, deceptive phenomena,
Hollow, empty, and without a self:
They see them as utterly solitary. <note>isolated from inherent existence</note>

Without a station, there is no focal point.
Without a root, they do not remain.
They arise entirely from the cause of ignorance,

<pb n="41"/>Completely devoid of beginning, middle, or end.
Like a plantain tree, they have no core.
They are like a city of <term>gandharvas</term> <gloss>celestial musicians; a metaphor for a mirage</gloss>.
The world, a terrible city of confusion,
Appears like a magical illusion.

What appears as truth to this world,
Including Brahma and the others,
The Noble Ones call "false."
What else remains but this?

The world is blinded by ignorance
And follows the current of craving.
How could the wise, free from craving,
Be the same as those who seek virtue? <note>referring to those seeking ordinary virtuous rebirth versus ultimate liberation</note>

To those searching for suchness, one should first
Say that "everything exists."
Once they understand the meanings and are without attachment,
Then later they are taught "solitude" <gloss>emptiness</gloss>.

Without knowing the meaning of solitude,
Those who merely follow what they have heard,
And who do not perform merit,
Those inferior people are ruined.

The fact that actions have results
And the realms of existence were also correctly taught.
The thorough knowledge of their nature
And their non-arising were also shown.

Just as the Victors spoke of "I" and "mine"
For the sake of a specific purpose,
So too the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases
Were taught for a specific purpose.

What was described as the great elements and so on
Is perfectly gathered within consciousness.
Since one is freed by knowing that,
Is it not falsely conceptualized?

The Victors have taught
That nirvana is the sole truth.
At that time, what wise person would think
That the rest is not false?

As long as the mind is wavering,
That is the domain of <term>Mara</term> <gloss>the tempter or personification of death and desire</gloss>.
If that is so, then why is it not logical
That there is no fault in this?

Because the Buddhas have taught
That the world has ignorance as its condition,
Why is it not logical that this world
Is a conceptualization?

When ignorance ceases,
That which ceases along with it—
How could it not be clear
That it was conceptualized from not knowing?

That which arises together with a cause
And does not remain without conditions,
And also perishes because of the absence of conditions—
How can it be understood to "exist"?

If those who speak of existence
Remain attached to the excellence of things,

<pb n="42"/>Remaining on that very path,
There is nothing wonderful about that.
But those who rely on the Buddha's path
And speak of everything as impermanent,
While grasping for the excellence of things through dispute—
That station is despised.

When, after investigating, one does not find
Anything that can be called "this" or "that,"
Which wise person would say
In dispute that "this" or "that" is true?

Those who, without reliance,
Are attached to a self or the world—
Alas, they are carried away by views
Such as "permanent," "impermanent," and so on.

Those who accept things
As established in suchness through reliance,
How could the faults of "inference" and so forth
Not arise for them?

Those who accept things through reliance
As being like the moon in water,
Neither real nor false—
They are not carried away by views.

If there is the acceptance of things as real,
Then the terrible and malicious views
Arising from desire and hatred will emerge,
And conduct arising from them will follow.

That acceptance is the cause of all views.
Without it, afflictions do not arise.
Therefore, if that is thoroughly known,
Views and afflictions will be completely purified.

If you wonder, "Who knows that
While there is the acceptance of things as real?"
One who sees dependent origination sees
That what is born through reliance is unborn.

This was taught by the Supreme Knower of Suchness.
It overcomes false knowledge.
The process of attachment, dispute, and so forth
Arising from "truth," "untruth," and "falsehood,"
Proceeds from attachment.

Those of great nature
Have no position and no dispute.
For those who have no position,
How could there be a counter-position?

Having found any kind of station,
One will be seized by the deceptive, poisonous snake of afflictions.
Those whose minds have no station
Will not be seized.

For those whose minds have a station,
Why would the great poison of afflictions not occur?
They will be seized by the snake of afflictions.
By perceiving things as true, children

Are attached to reflections.
In the same way, because the world is confused,

<pb n="43"/>It becomes trapped in the snare of objects.
The Great Beings see things
With the eye of wisdom as being like reflections;
They are not trapped in the mud
Of what are called "objects."

Children are attached to forms;
The moderate become free from attachment.
Those possessed of the highest intellect, who know
The nature of form, are liberated.

Attachment arises from thinking something is beautiful;
By reversing that, one is free from desire.
By seeing things as solitary, like a magical person,
One will pass into nirvana.

Whatever faults of affliction there are
That torment through false knowledge—
The conceptualization of existence and non-existence—
Do not arise for one who knows the meaning.

If there were a station, there would be attachment
And freedom from attachment;
But the Great Beings who have no station
Are neither attached nor free from attachment.

Those whose wavering minds do not waver
Even when thinking of "solitude" <gloss>emptiness</gloss>,
Have crossed the inexhaustible ocean of existence
Which is agitated by the snake of afflictions.

Through this virtue, may all beings
Accumulate the collections of merit and wisdom;
From that merit and wisdom, may they obtain
The two supreme goals <note>The Form Body and Truth Body of a Buddha</note>.

The Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning, composed by the master Noble Nagarjuna, is complete. It was corrected and established by the Indian scholar Muditashri and the Tibetan translator Pa tshab Nyi ma grags.

In the language of India: <term>Vaidalyasūtra-nāma</term> <gloss>The Finely Woven Sutra</gloss>.
In the language of Tibet: <term>Zhib mo rnam par 'thag pa zhes bya ba'i mdo</term>.
Homage to the master Noble Nagarjuna.

For those who desire to dispute
Through the pride of knowing logic,
In order to abandon that pride,
I shall explain the <term>Vaidalyaprakaraṇa</term> <gloss>The Finely Woven Treatise</gloss>.

The means of valid cognition and the objects of cognition are both intertwined. This is because they are not established from their own side. Existence, non-existence, and both are not dependent. They are not, because it would follow that there is no end.
</translation>

<summary>This text contains the concluding verses of Nagarjuna's Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning, which argues that liberation is achieved by seeing through the illusions of existence and non-existence via dependent origination. It transitions into the beginning of his Vaidalya Sutra, a critique of formal logic intended to humble those proud of their debating skills.</summary>

<keywords>Nagarjuna, Middle Way, dependent origination, emptiness, nirvana, logic, Vaidalyasutra, Yuktisastika, Madhyamaka</keywords>

That which arises together with a cause
And does not remain without conditions,
And also perishes because of the absence of conditions—
How can it be understood to "exist"?

If those who speak of existence
Remain attached to the excellence of things,
pages.head: They arise entirely from the cause of ignorance,
pages.tail:
Remaining on that very path,
There is nothing wonderful about that.

pages.span:
Remaining on that very path,
There is nothing wonderful about that.
But those who rely on the Buddha's path
And speak of everything as impermanent,
While grasping for the excellence of things through dispute—
That station is despised.

When, after investigating, one does not find
Anything that can be called "this" or "that,"
Which wise person would say
In dispute that "this" or "that" is true?

Those who, without reliance,
Are attached to a self or the world—
Alas, they are carried away by views
Such as "permanent," "impermanent," and so on.

Those who accept things
As established in suchness through reliance,
How could the faults of "inference" and so forth
Not arise for them?

Those who accept things through reliance
As being like the moon in water,
Neither real nor false—
They are not carried away by views.

If there is the acceptance of things as real,
Then the terrible and malicious views
Arising from desire and hatred will emerge,
And conduct arising from them will follow.

That acceptance is the cause of all views.
Without it, afflictions do not arise.
Therefore, if that is thoroughly known,
Views and afflictions will be completely purified.

If you wonder, "Who knows that
While there is the acceptance of things as real?"
One who sees dependent origination sees
That what is born through reliance is unborn.

This was taught by the Supreme Knower of Suchness.
It overcomes false knowledge.
The process of attachment, dispute, and so forth
Arising from "truth," "untruth," and "falsehood,"
Proceeds from attachment.

Those of great nature
Have no position and no dispute.
For those who have no position,
How could there be a counter-position?

Having found any kind of station,
One will be seized by the deceptive, poisonous snake of afflictions.
Those whose minds have no station
Will not be seized.

For those whose minds have a station,
Why would the great poison of afflictions not occur?
They will be seized by the snake of afflictions.
By perceiving things as true, children

Are attached to reflections.
In the same way, because the world is confused,
pages.head:
If those who speak of existence
Remain attached to the excellence of things,
pages.tail: It becomes trapped in the snare of objects.

pages.span:
It becomes trapped in the snare of objects.
The Great Beings see things
With the eye of wisdom as being like reflections;
They are not trapped in the mud
Of what are called "objects."

Children are attached to forms;
The moderate become free from attachment.
Those possessed of the highest intellect, who know
The nature of form, are liberated.

Attachment arises from thinking something is beautiful;
By reversing that, one is free from desire.
By seeing things as solitary, like a magical person,
One will pass into nirvana.

Whatever faults of affliction there are
That torment through false knowledge—
The conceptualization of existence and non-existence—
Do not arise for one who knows the meaning.

If there were a station, there would be attachment
And freedom from attachment;
But the Great Beings who have no station
Are neither attached nor free from attachment.

Those whose wavering minds do not waver
Even when thinking of "solitude" <gloss>emptiness</gloss>,
Have crossed the inexhaustible ocean of existence
Which is agitated by the snake of afflictions.

Through this virtue, may all beings
Accumulate the collections of merit and wisdom;
From that merit and wisdom, may they obtain
The two supreme goals <note>The Form Body and Truth Body of a Buddha</note>.

The Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning, composed by the master Noble Nagarjuna, is complete. It was corrected and established by the Indian scholar Muditashri and the Tibetan translator Pa tshab Nyi ma grags.

In the language of India: <term>Vaidalyasūtra-nāma</term> <gloss>The Finely Woven Sutra</gloss>.
In the language of Tibet: <term>Zhib mo rnam par 'thag pa zhes bya ba'i mdo</term>.
Homage to the master Noble Nagarjuna.

For those who desire to dispute
Through the pride of knowing logic,
In order to abandon that pride,
I shall explain the <term>Vaidalyaprakaraṇa</term> <gloss>The Finely Woven Treatise</gloss>.

The means of valid cognition and the objects of cognition are both intertwined. This is because they are not established from their own side. Existence, non-existence, and both are not dependent. They are not, because it would follow that there is no end.
